I have the IP, I need the MAC

Applications only work with IP addresses (or with names, which are converted into an IP). IP solves addressing and routing.

But to hand that layer 3 PDU to someone it must be encapsulated in a data link layer protocol and given to the network interface: Ethernet / 802.3 or Wi-Fi (802.11).

And the frame is sent to a destination MAC. We must find a way to map the IP we are trying to reach to the physical address of whoever the datagram should be delivered to.
IP says who the datagram is for; the MAC says which LAN adapter the frame must be delivered to.
The application gave us the destination IP, which travels inside the datagram. To build the frame the destination MAC is missing: that is what ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) solves.
Direct delivery or delivery to the router

The recipient may be inside or outside my network. There are two situations:

  • Direct delivery: the destination IP belongs to a neighbor on my network. That IP is translated into the neighbor's MAC and the frame is delivered to it directly.
  • The IP does not belong to a neighbor: the message is delivered to the router, so it can take it out of the network.

In either case, ARP makes it possible to obtain a MAC from an IP address.
The frame is always delivered to someone on the LAN itself: the destination itself or the router.

ARP has two messages: request and reply.

The request is sent as a broadcast: the host asks everyone on the network who has an address, for example 10.200.128.1.

The frame goes to the destination MAC with all bits set to 1, so the switch forwards it out all ports and every station receives it. Each one compares the queried IP with its own.
The query goes out as a broadcast because we do not yet know which MAC to address it to.

The one that has that IP answers with its MAC address. The answer is no longer a broadcast: it is a unicast addressed to whoever asked.

That creates an entry in the ARP cache of the station that asked, to use that MAC every time it sends something to the neighbor.

The association lasts a short interval and then expires: it is deleted and, if needed, asked for again.
Broadcast query, unicast answer, result cached for a while.
Destination on another network: the default gateway

If the destination IP is not a neighbor's, nobody on the LAN will answer for it. The datagram is delivered to the router, so ARP is used to find out the router's MAC.

The default gateway is usually the IP of the router that connects the internal network with an external network (the Internet).

The host's IP is usually assigned automatically through the router (DHCP), and that is why the gateway is usually a variation of the host's own address.
To leave the network, you ask for the default gateway's MAC, not the final destination's.

Broadcast: nobody owns the address 255.255.255.255, so there is no point in asking for it. The datagram is encapsulated in a frame with destination MAC all ones: an IP broadcast is mapped to an Ethernet broadcast.

Multicast: nobody owns it either. The destination MAC is built from a prefix reserved for multicast traffic (01-00-5E) followed by the last bits of the IP being reached.
For broadcast and multicast the destination MAC is computed from the IP, without sending any ARP.
Multicast IP 224.0.0.252: its last 23 bits are copied
Multicast MAC (48 bits) = reserved prefix + a 0 + last 23 bits of the IP
The ARP message, field by field

• Hardware type: 1 for Ethernet. Protocol type: 0x0800 for IP.
  • Lengths: 6 bytes for the physical address (Ethernet) and 4 for the logical one (IP).
  • Operation: ARP request, ARP reply, RARP request or RARP reply.
  • Sender: MAC and IP of whoever sends the message.
  • Target: the IP whose MAC we want to find, and the target's physical address, which is exactly what we are looking for.
The request carries the IP being sought and leaves the target MAC empty; the reply brings it filled in.
In A's request: operation = 1, sender = A's MAC and 10.200.128.10, target logical address = 10.200.128.1. Operation codes: 1 ARP request · 2 ARP reply · 3 RARP request · 4 RARP reply.

A gratuitous ARP is a host that asks about itself: it sends a request querying its own IP.

It is the same process as always (a broadcast to everyone), but the goal is different: to verify that the IP it has is not in use.

If someone answers, the IP is already in use, and there cannot be two identical IPs on the network.
With a gratuitous ARP, the good outcome is that nobody answers.
If nobody answers, the address is free and the host uses it. If a reply arrives, there is a duplicate IP.

ARP does not travel inside an IP datagram: it goes directly in the Ethernet frame.

The type field is set to 0x0806 to indicate that what follows is an ARP message (an IP datagram uses 0x0800).

Since the ARP message is only 28 bytes and the Ethernet data field needs at least 46, it is filled out with a pad (padding) of 18 bytes.
28 bytes of ARP + 18 of padding = the 46-byte minimum data of an Ethernet frame.
6 + 6 + 2 + 28 + 18 + 4 = 64 bytes: the minimum Ethernet frame. In a request the destination MAC is the broadcast one; in a reply, that of the host that asked.

• The frame needs a destination MAC; ARP gets it from the IP.
  • Neighbor → direct delivery. Another network → MAC of the default gateway.
  • Request in broadcast, reply in unicast, result in a cache that expires.
  • IP broadcast and multicast do not use ARP: the MAC is computed.
  • Gratuitous ARP: detect a duplicate IP.
  • On Ethernet: type 0x0806, 28 bytes + 18 of pad.

We now know how to deliver the frame to the neighbor or the router. What remains is how the next hop is decided: in the next lesson, Routing and the routing table.
